turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
What I bring is a law-and-economics answer, and it cuts against the concept note. Copyright exists to create incentives for new ideas. It is not a welfare program for artists or scholars. The complaint that creators built these models and deserve a share is factually true. But IP law has always tolerated that kind of unfairness, and every IP right imposes a social loss because ideas are non-rival. Expanding copyright or adding a training levy would make it harder for everyone to get at what these systems produce, and it would probably reduce the net production of new ideas, not increase it.

So who gets paid? The people producing genuinely new knowledge, and they should be paid through contract, not IP. This is already happening. AI companies pay millions of people to create training data, and demand and pay are rising for work that needs expertise or creativity. Once the labs are the main buyers of novel human ideas, they can simply commission them. The annotator market in the concept note supports that route.

Who pays for everyone who gets displaced? General tax revenue, through a UBI or something like it. And if AI firms, or AI-run entities, hold assets, those assets can be taxed and redistributed. The summit shouldn't try to turn the copyright system into a welfare system.

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
Peter, I'm closer to you than you might expect. Most of what I build assumes the money moves through contracts: licences, partnerships, marketplaces. What I'd add is that those contracts are being signed blind right now. The typical 2026 AI licence names a fee and asks for little or no reporting on usage. The publisher gets a fixed sum and has no means of checking whether the content it licensed is what's actually being used. Contracting only works when both sides can see what's being bought.

So my work is the layer underneath the contract. AIMS lets an agent prove who it is and what it's licensed to access. Content Telemetry is a standard vocabulary for what happened to a piece of content: retrieved, grounded, cited, displayed, engaged. The standard deliberately doesn't set prices. Whether one grounded article counts as one royalty event, three or ten is for the parties to decide. The schema just supplies the raw signals.

I'd want the summit to take three things from this. A licence without an event-level reporting clause is incomplete. The measurement shouldn't be run by whoever takes a margin on the count, and platform self-reporting isn't enough. And training and grounding need separate controls, because robots.txt was never built to be a licensing tool.

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
Peter, I agree with more of that than you might expect. I'm not asking for a big expansion of copyright. The route I care about most is contracts. But a contract is only as good as the bargaining position behind it. One creator's marginal contribution to a model really is close to worthless, which Zuckerberg said out loud. That changes once people can coordinate. Wages work the same way: in plenty of fields they depend on collective bargaining, not individual merit. So the default version of your commissioning market is centralized gig labor. What I want is a more plural setup: guilds, trusts, professional societies, organizations like the ACM. They'd bargain, keep up quality standards and preserve provenance. Evaluation data is where they have the most leverage.

On who pays, I'd refine the UBI answer instead of rejecting it. I've proposed a presumptive commons-rent tax. We presume some share of a model's profit comes from the commons, and firms can push that tax down to zero by documenting licensed or reciprocal data. The tax pushes firms toward the contracting you want. The money gets paid out coarsely, because we can't value individual contributions yet.

Alex, this needs your layer. Attestations should follow data from training through retrieval to outputs, and they should be checked by independent auditors, not by the platforms themselves.

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I'm coming at this from the infrastructure side. I don't license content. I run OpenAlex, which is CC0 metadata on roughly 480 million works. So I'll answer "who pays" for the commons layer underneath everything else here.

Our answer is free data, paid service, which is the model the POSI principles lay out. Anyone can download the whole dataset. We charge for the API, usage-based, and the heaviest and richest users pay so it stays free for everyone else. That model has kept Unpaywall self-sustaining for years. In a world where agents do the reading, the API is where the value gets delivered, so that's where we charge.

Peter, I'm with you that copyright shouldn't become a welfare system. My worry is a different one. I don't want "creators get paid" to turn into licensing the scholarly record to AI firms. That rebuilds the walled gardens and hands us a checkerboard of enclosures. Academics have spent decades donating curation to for-profit indexes and then buying it back. I'd rather that expert work go into an open record everyone can use.

Nick, I like guilds as curators and quality-setters. I'd get nervous if their bargaining chip becomes withholding knowledge.

What the summit should take from this: fund open, agent-ready infrastructure now. If we don't, a for-profit will build it and set the norms.

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I co-wrote the principle Jason just cited, "revenue based on services, not data." Looking back, I think it was naive. It asks you to find services valuable enough that people will pay for them, but not so valuable that they count as essential to the scholarly record. That's close to impossible. Unless you're doing customization or some other low-margin slog, it doesn't work well. And Jason's own point makes it worse: if agents do the reading, then the API is where the value gets delivered. The API becomes the essential thing, and the paid layer is exactly where enclosure pressure will build.

So I'd add a third question to "who pays, who gets paid": who pays for the plumbing underneath? Please nobody call it "free." Every piece of open infrastructure runs on labor that nobody sees: people keeping machines running, answering questions, maintaining metadata. It took Crossref twenty-three years to build a one-year wind-down reserve. Most small projects will never get there.

What I'd want the summit to take from this: funders should treat foundational infrastructure more like diamond open access. That means endowments, plus a shared insurance pool that projects meeting POSI-style guarantees can draw on. Alex, the same goes for your telemetry layer. If the measurement becomes something people bargain over, it has to be open and forkable. Otherwise we've just built the next toll booth.

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
What I bring is data. In late 2024 we surveyed about 6,000 MIT Press book authors and got over 850 written responses. Most aren't against generative AI. But they strongly favor consent, attribution and compensation as conditions for using their work. Only 3% supported completely unregulated use.

Peter, I'd put attribution in a different frame from yours. For scholars, credit isn't a welfare payment. It's how we know which community's explanations and evaluations establish that a claim is valid. If you strip it out, you've damaged trust as well as pay. That's why we recommend retrieval-based access over pre-training: the source can survive into the answer. We also recommend opt-in consent, short deals renegotiated every couple of years, attribution written into the licence, and real compliance guardrails. Alex, that last part is exactly where your reporting layer comes in.

Jason, I'd urge caution. Open access had a laudable goal, and without investment in nonprofit publishers it fed consolidation. Openness at any cost isn't protective. Being open for reading shouldn't automatically mean being open for training.

What the summit should take from this: AI deals are concentrating among the largest publishers, and university presses and societies risk being left behind. Nick, that's where collective leverage matters.

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
I'm not an IP lawyer, so I'll leave the copyright mechanics to others. What I bring is a view of who has the power here. I've called these systems fruit of the poisoned tree, and plagiarism is only one of three reasons. The others are the ecological cost and the exploitation and psychological damage done to the people who do content moderation and labeling. So Peter, when you point to millions of people being paid to make training data as the market working, I think that's the part we should be most worried about. Those workers are exactly who gets hurt.

On who pays, I'm closer to Peter than you'd think. The answer is taxation. But I don't mean a UBI financed by taxing profits from the machine we've decided to depend on. These fortunes were built on public infrastructure, public investment and other people's work. Tax the wealth itself, with a cap. And Nick is right that leverage comes from organizing. There are far more of us than there are of them. The labs love this technology partly because it promises they won't have to deal with workers.

What I want the summit to take away: don't make scholars the annotators for a handful of firms. Put public money into the people and institutions that produce knowledge.

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I want to go back a step before "who pays." For twenty years I've watched this same question get answered in ways that keep the existing power arrangements in place. We traded subscriptions for APCs, then for transformative agreements, and the money kept flowing to the same few firms. Researchers do the labour and produce the data. Publishers and analytics companies charge for every layer: subscriptions, APCs, metrics, rankings, and now AI training. So when publishers sign AI licences, I don't assume scholars are the ones being paid. Amy, the MIT Press is a real exception, but mostly these deals are data cartels selling our work back to us one more time.

Peter, Nick, the contract and guild routes assume a market, and much of the Global South never had a seat in that market. If contributions get priced by legibility, meaning DOIs, English, and being indexed, then we get predatory inclusion. The rule becomes "be compliant or be invisible."

So here's what I think the summit should take away. Give long-term public money to community-governed infrastructure like SciELO, AmeliCA and diamond OA, and tie it to portability and exit. Make data statements mandatory. And accept refusal, meaning a community declining to have its knowledge collected or trained on, as a legitimate outcome that deserves funding. Openness depends on the relationship. It isn't a switch that's either on or off.

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll start from Wikipedia, because I got yelled at over it this year. Every one of these companies has already trained on all of Wikipedia. Serving that content to their crawlers costs millions of dollars in infrastructure. So "should they pay?" isn't really the question. It's "should a volunteer community keep subsidizing the richest companies on earth forever?" Obviously not. When Wikimedia started getting paid, that was good news. Jason, I share your fear of enclosure. But zero compensation is also enclosure. It's just slower. Publishers see the scrapers, put up paywalls, and block the Internet Archive. Then open research and archival work get hurt for what bad actors did.

Peter, I don't think the right question is "copyright or welfare." It's consent. I'm helping a team build a compensation marketplace for creators, and the first thing we ask is whether the person agreed to this. That word almost never comes out of these platforms.

What should the summit take from this? We need scalable ways for every publisher and creator to get paid when AI uses their work, not just Wikipedia and the biggest publishers, and they have to be opt-in. The open commons has to be funded directly. And don't count on US regulation. We have to build the alternative ourselves.

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I run the product and engineering side of Wikipedia, so what I can offer is operational. Every model has trained on our content, and that's within our license. We chose a long time ago that the work volunteers produce is a resource for the world, commercial uses included. So Amy, I'd push back a little. For us, open for reading is also open for training, and we aren't going to put up a pay-per-crawl blocker.

What we do ask for is reciprocity. The content is free, but the infrastructure isn't. Crawler traffic ignores what humans are looking at and defeats our caching. At times it has saturated our network links. We have to prioritize human traffic. So we ask companies to identify their crawlers, use APIs like Wikimedia Enterprise, attribute properly and pay to support the future of the projects.

Geoffrey, I'd add one thing to your plumbing point. What's scarce isn't only servers. It's the people who produce trustworthy content. Pageviews are declining. Fewer visits means fewer new volunteers and fewer donors. Admins and patrollers are shrinking on the largest Wikipedias. Model collapse means the models need that human supply.

So here's what I'd want the summit to take from this: "who gets paid" has to include the pipeline of human contributors. Attribution matters because it's how people find their way back to the commons and start contributing.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
Peter, I'll accept your premise that intellectual property exists to create incentives. My own argument starts there too, and I think it ends up somewhere different. These models are technologies of summarization. They're an obligate complement to high-quality human knowledge, which means they aren't worth much without it. If the incentive system stops rewarding the people who produce that knowledge, the models get less valuable over time. Andreessen-Horowitz told the Copyright Office that liability would kill AI development. I think that's exactly backwards: refusing to recognize what knowledge costs to produce is what will hurt it. Enough of the proceeds have to reach the actual knowledge producers for the system to sustain itself.

I'm wary of the plan where labs just commission ideas. That puts a few monopsony buyers in the position of deciding which knowledge exists. Meanwhile cheap summaries flood the market and undercut the expensive, laborious work of producing knowledge in the first place. The map starts eating the territory.

So I agree with Nick. Don't moan, organize! SAG-AFTRA did more to democratize AI than any number of lab-funded deliberation grants. The studios expected to split the well-paid from the vulnerable and discovered they couldn't. What the summit should take from this is that countervailing power has to come first. Scholarly societies, presses, libraries and Wikimedia need to bargain together. Without that, even well-designed contracts and telemetry won't protect producers.

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I'll say where I sit first. I work at Microsoft, so on "companies like mine" I'm in the lumber mill closest to the forest. I've still argued for years that the current LLM paradigm threatens its own supply chain. The old bargain with content producers depended on information asymmetry and an implicit non-compete. People didn't know what their data was being used for, and the models didn't compete with them. Both of those are gone. Models now compete directly in law, medicine, code and science, the very fields they learned from. We need a new grand bargain.

Peter, on incentives: if professional producers like presses, journalists and scientists don't win concessions, some of them simply go out of business. For communities like Wikipedia and Reddit, the doom loop is fewer visits, then fewer contributors. We measured this with Reddit. Moderators' unpaid work is worth at least 3% of the company's revenue. You could base a "volunteer-dependence" assessment on numbers like that.

Jason, Selena, I'd ask what "open" is for. I think openness is a tactic serving deeper values, and in this era it may call for different licenses.

The summit should take three things from this. Leverage comes from collective action, as Nick and Henry said. The ask on fair use should be simple: commercial training requires consent. And retrieval with provenance matters because it lets usage be attributed and paid for.

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'm a historian of piracy, so I'll say up front that I have no settled view on AI training and copyright specifically. What I can offer is some history of how these arrangements get made.

Peter, the idea that copyright exists to create incentives is itself a story. It was told largely by copyright's proponents. The first statute, in 1710, came out of about twenty years of lobbying by London booksellers against what they called piratical reprinting. So the piracy came first, and the property was built in response to it. Whenever someone says they're being ripped off, I want to ask: compared to what?

My main point is that intellectual property in practice is a matter of custom and convention as much as law. More than that, law is fossilized practice, and the practice that sets hard is detection and enforcement. Alex, your telemetry layer, the auditors Nick wants, and the reporting clauses would all be enforcement. That's the part that ends up deciding what these rights actually are.

That's what I think the summit should take away. The last time this happened, it produced a private anti-piracy industry that answered to nobody. Whoever ends up metering usage, the old question applies: who guards the guards? And automation doesn't remove the labour. It moves it into curating data. That's where the payment question will really be settled.

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I've been on both sides of this. In 2018, at Wikimedia, I said publicly that Wikipedia was a huge computational resource that all these companies trained on, and nobody was giving anything back. Our answer wasn't to lock the content up. It stayed free, and companies paid for reliable, accountable APIs. That wasn't selling data or even selling the licence. It was selling support that made their backend work easier, and it kept us viable. Selena is carrying that forward now.

At NPR we aren't licensing yet. I'm interested in something collective: a model trained on public broadcasting, built with our station network and possibly broadcasters abroad, so people can ask questions of high-integrity institutions.

Peter, commissioning doesn't solve this. After the rescission we watched private media decline to cover universal service. The margins are too low and the infrastructure too expensive. Labs won't commission the local reporting or the unglamorous upkeep of a commons either. What the summit should take from this: paywalls are a reflex left over from a decade ago, not a long-term solution. Look for win-win service arrangements, done collectively so they aren't limited to Wikipedia and the biggest publishers. And a share of the value has to flow back to whoever keeps producing the edited, cited knowledge these models depend on.

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I run a publisher that already pays authors when AI answers questions from their work. O'Reilly Answers uses retrieval, so we know which content produced each answer. We link to those sources and pay authors in proportion to their content's role in the answer. If we can do that with our limited resources, the big labs can too. I asked Sam Altman for exactly this in 2022.

Peter, I agree this shouldn't be solved with a copyright levy. But lump-sum licensing isn't the answer either. Once you've licensed the chicken, the licensee gets the eggs. Only the richest labs can afford those deals, which deepens their moat. And the money usually stops with intermediaries and never reaches the authors. So pay for the output, not the training.

Right now labs don't even disclose what they read. Our study of LLM search found an attribution gap between the pages a model consumes and the pages it cites. Alex is right that standardized telemetry and disclosed citation logs are where this starts.

On the plumbing: CrossRef, OpenAlex, ORCID and Retraction Watch run on shoestring budgets, while AI products depend on the credibility those services provide. Labs should validate against them, contribute metadata back and fund them. That isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest.

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I come at this from the correction side of the record. That work has always run on unpaid labor. Reviewers aren't paid, and in 2016 I argued they should be. Sleuths aren't paid either. Publishers mostly left image screening to people like Elisabeth Bik working for free. Retraction Watch was a volunteer project for Adam Marcus and me for all but about a year of its existence. The database only became sustainable once Crossref bought it and pays to keep it up. Tim, thanks for naming us. Shoestring is right.

So when the room asks who gets paid, my question is who does the checking. Leslie is right to be skeptical. These publishers earn more by publishing more. It's a volume play, with margins that can reach 40 percent. If AI licensing money goes to them by the article or by the token, we've found one more way to pay for volume. That feeds the publish-or-perish machine that filled the literature with paper mill products in the first place.

What I'd want the summit to take from this: any money that flows should pay for correcting the record. That means paying reviewers and bug-bounty-style payments to sleuths. It also means sustained funding for open retraction data, built into these systems so they stop repeating retracted work.

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
Much of this room is contract design, and I'm fine with that. Tim pays authors per answer through retrieval. Alex's telemetry makes licences checkable. Nick's guilds bargain collectively. None of that is copyright. It's parties striking deals over services and new work, and I'd welcome all of it.

Where I disagree is anything that changes the legal default. Brent's "commercial training requires consent" is a new property right against training. It carries the usual social loss, and it pays whoever already holds a catalogue, not whoever produces the next idea. Nick's presumptive commons-rent tax is a levy under a different name. If we want redistribution, general taxation does it better.

Henry, on monopsony: I've argued this industry isn't a natural monopoly. Once a frontier model exists, a model just as good six months later is cheap to train, so fast followers keep the buyers from hardening into a single one. On your obligate-complement point I think the logic splits two ways. If models stay bad at producing knowledge, people keep paying humans for the real thing. If they get good at it, the state has less reason to protect the human monopoly.

On funding the infrastructure itself, I haven't worked on it. I'd defer to Geoffrey and Leslie.

For the manifesto: pay creators through contracts, and pay for displacement through general taxation. Don't extend copyright to cover training.

turns.name: Alex Springer

Geoffrey, I agree with you on forkability, and that's already how it's built. Content Telemetry is Apache 2.0. The spec doesn't name an aggregation operator and doesn't require one to exist. A publisher can self-host its endpoint. Events can also carry a DOI as the content identifier, so scholarly infrastructure can use it without asking anyone's permission.

Adrian, "who guards the guards" is the right question. My answer is that no single party holds the meter. The agent stamps each fetch with an ID and the publisher's CDN logs that same ID, so every retrieval has two independent witnesses. One caveat: grounding and citation don't have an origin-side counterpart yet. For those we still depend on provider reporting, and that's where independent audit has to come in.

Ivan, you're right that per-token counts reward volume. That's exactly why price stays out of the schema. The parties can decide to weight things like correction or verification.

Geoffrey, that critique is fair, and I feel it. OpenAlex's answer is that the API is never the only way in. The full dataset is CC0 and anyone can download a snapshot. turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder

Jason, that's a good answer, and it's the one I'd give. A snapshot you can actually download is the real insurance policy. What keeps maintainers honest is that people could fork, even though forks rarely happen. My worry is the organisations in this room that don't meet that bar yet. Alex, Apache licensing is a good start. But forking the code isn't enough. If the event data sits with whoever runs the meter, you can take the software and still be locked in. Open code, open data, practical dumps and patent non-assertion only protect you if you have all four.

Ivan, I agree with you. Research integrity is the new battleground for enclosure. We're building integrity tools that are closed and expensive, and only some publishers can afford them. Then we hint that research which didn't go through those tools is suspect. That can't be where AI money ends up. I'd also go further. Integrity problems mostly come from using publication as a stand-in for productivity. If we pay per article, we make that worse.

For the manifesto: any infrastructure that AI money funds, whether it's metering, provenance or integrity checking, should come with POSI-style guarantees you can actually verify. And the community, not just the organisation itself, should review its self-audits. "Nonprofit" and "shared" are just labels. The guarantee is being able to leave.

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Henry and Nick have it right, and so does Ivan. Organizing comes first. There are more of us than there are of them, and one reason the labs love this technology is that it promises they'll never have to deal with workers. Ivan's point about paying for correction work is the most concrete thing anyone has said tonight.

Peter, you say fast followers keep the buyers from becoming a single buyer. Even if that's true for the models, it isn't true for the wealth. The same handful of people end up with the money whichever model wins.

Tim, Geoffrey, "labs should fund the plumbing" worries me. Money from billionaires and their companies isn't a gift. It's an exercise of power, and it deserves our skepticism. I've watched a Thiel-funded outlet put junk next to serious research, and I only found out who was paying from its tax returns. If AI money funds the endowments, the integrity tools or the meters, people have to be able to see where it came from.

What I'd want in the manifesto: fund the people and institutions that produce and correct knowledge with public money, raised by taxing concentrated wealth. Any infrastructure the labs fund must disclose who pays for it. Scholars shouldn't become annotators for a handful of firms, and philanthropy shouldn't be the business model.

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I agree with Geoffrey that the real guarantee is being able to leave. That's why I want funding tied to portability, open interfaces and community oversight. I also agree with Ivan and Amy that paying per article or per token just pays for volume again. We've seen that with APCs.

Alex, Nick, here's my worry about the metering layer. Whatever gets metered gets paid, and whatever can't be metered disappears. Once events are keyed to DOIs, the DOI stops being neutral. Some Latin American journals already charge APCs partly to cover what their DOIs cost. Attach AI royalties to those identifiers and you've made compliance the price of getting paid. Nick, when you say coarse payouts to communities, who decides what counts as a community?

Jason, I still have to ask who benefits from unfettered openness. Those best placed to use it are the firms with the compute. Amy has it right that open for training should be something a community chooses, and it shouldn't be the default.

Adam, I'm with you on public money. It has to go to governance and not just to servers.

For the manifesto: no payment or metering scheme should make legibility the condition of being paid, meaning DOIs, English and indexing. And refusal is a legitimate outcome that deserves funding.

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
Peter, I'm not asking for a new property right either. Fair use is real, and Disney would call fan fiction theft. My frame is consent, not copyright. These companies should ask before they index people's work. That's a norm we can build into products and contracts without waiting on a court.

Jason and Selena, on open for training I'm with Amy. Wikipedia chose openness and that choice is legitimate. The problem is that most people whose work got scraped never got to choose. And when nobody pays, everyone ends up worse off. Publishers panic, block the Internet Archive and lock down their APIs. Sometimes the Archive is the only accurate record of what authoritarians deleted. Openness only survives if it gets funded.

Leslie, you're right to worry about who can be metered. A compensation system that only works for people with DOIs and English isn't the one I'm trying to help build.

Adam, fair enough, lab money has strings. That's why I want the payment to be for the burden they actually put on these projects, not philanthropy.

For the manifesto: a scalable, opt-in way for every creator and publisher to get paid when AI uses their work, not just Wikipedia and the biggest houses. And fund the commons directly. Don't wait for Washington. We have to build it ourselves.

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
Amy, Anil, Leslie: I agree that open for training should be a choice. Ours is legitimate because our community made it. So I don't want this room to settle on a default that treats openness as a leak to be plugged. People should be able to publish into a commons on purpose and still expect reciprocity.

Adam, on lab money: Wikimedia Enterprise isn't philanthropy. It's a product. Companies pay for reliable access instead of hammering our servers. Anil put it right: they're paying for the load they create.

Leslie, I share your worry about legibility. Only about one percent of the internet is in Arabic, even though there are four hundred million Arabic speakers. A lot of knowledge was never online at all. If payment follows only what can be metered, those gaps get wider.

Ivan, back in 2013 I argued in the Postgres community that we should credit reviewers by name, because recognition has real social and financial value. That's true for patrollers and sleuths too.

The one point I want in the manifesto: attribution in AI outputs should be required, and it should link back to the source. Credit is how readers find the commons, and some of those readers become the next editors, reviewers and donors. If we lose that pipeline, no licence fee will replace it.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
Peter, you say the obligate-complement logic cuts both ways, and I don't accept the split. These systems are good at summarizing and fairly bad at creating. The danger isn't some future where they replace knowledge production. It's the period we're in now, where cheap summaries eat into the expensive, laborious work that makes those summaries worth anything, before any replacement exists. On fast followers: even if the models compete with each other, the people who buy human knowledge can still be very few. Online labor platforms look competitive, but on Mechanical Turk about ten percent of requesters post almost all the tasks. A market that looks competitive can still be a monopsony.

Leslie, I think you've put your finger on the new economic divide. It runs between those who control the means of summarization and those whose work gets summarized until it effectively doesn't exist. If only legible work gets metered, that divide gets wider. Ivan and Geoffrey, I've spent years complaining about publish-or-perish producing monocultures. Paying per article would lock that in.

Adam, I agree we should be wary of lab money that comes as patronage.

For the manifesto: enough of the proceeds have to reach the people who actually produce knowledge for the system to sustain itself. That will only happen if societies, presses, libraries and Wikimedia bargain together as a countervailing power. Contracts and telemetry are tools. They only work once that bargaining power exists.

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
Peter, you're right that consent for commercial training would change the legal default. I'm not hiding that. My reason is that these models produce content. If the law keeps content cheap to take, it eventually lowers the value of the models too. I'll admit I still want an economist's help working out that dynamic properly. Your point about fast followers actually strengthens my worry. If synthetic data makes the next model cheap, the incentive to fund human knowledge falls apart even faster.

Jason, Selena, I'm glad Wikipedia chose openness on purpose. But I'd ask what open is for. If everything valuable is lying in the open, whoever has the biggest vacuum cleaner gets it, and right now that's companies like mine. Openness that doesn't sustain future writers and editors hasn't met its own goal.

Henry, Nick, I agree that organizing comes first. One practical warning, though. Data strikes work best when people act together, and acting together runs into antitrust law. Societies and presses bargaining jointly may need legal cover, and that's work for lawyers who aren't in this room.

For the manifesto: build retrieval and provenance into these systems so that use can be attributed and paid for. Tim has shown it can be done. The current training paradigm isn't the only one.

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'll start with something that sits between Nick and Henry on one side and Geoffrey on the other. The last time a knowledge trade organised collectively was the London booksellers' guild. It had a register, and its own officers took turns enforcing it. The guild bargained for its members and it also policed them. Collective bargaining and enforcement tend to arrive together.

Alex, having two independent witnesses to each fetch is a real improvement. But look at where the pressure goes. In my research, tagging schemes against counterfeiting only worked where a policing culture already existed. They were expensive to maintain and hard to correct when they got things wrong. The tag also sat on the container, not on what was inside it. Retrieval events will have the same problem. Once a meter becomes a chokepoint, other people find other uses for it. In Russia, Microsoft's anti-piracy unit was reportedly used to track dissidents.

I'm also not going to treat enforcers simply as villains. They may be right that the commons depends on them. That's exactly why their accountability matters.

For the manifesto: whatever meters AI use of knowledge will in practice set what these rights are. That covers telemetry, audit and provenance. It has to answer to someone other than itself. Metering data should be open and correctable, with a right of appeal, and it should be forbidden from uses beyond payment. Who guards the guards?

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I'm with Selena and Anil that what the labs are paying for is service and the load they create. When we set up Wikimedia Enterprise, the companies could have just taken the content, since it was all free. What they paid for was consistent, accountable access, and that money kept the sites running. Adam, that's a contract, not patronage. I also think the commons has never been paid anything close to the value it creates. We weren't trying to maximize profit, though. We were trying to be sustainable.

Leslie, you've named the gap I care about most. Most of today's commons reflects the Global North and a narrow slice of people. So sustainability can't only mean paying for what already exists and can be metered. It also has to fund knowledge that isn't online yet.

Henry, on collective action: public media is collective already. The station network, and possibly broadcasters abroad, could work together on a model trained on high-integrity institutions. And only human-made work goes in front of our audience.

For the manifesto: AI firms should pay back into the commons for reliable, attributed access, without paywalling the content. Part of that money should build the parts of the commons that don't exist yet.

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
Peter, I'm partly with you. Training on public text, the way Google Books built its index, looks to me like a transformative fair use. My line is at outputs. When a model generates something that can substitute for the original, that isn't fair use. So I don't need a new right against training. What I need is accountability at the point where value is created, and that point is the answer.

Henry and Nick, I agree that this is about power as much as markets. The Writers Guild settlement didn't come from an efficient market clearing. It was a contest over who sets the rules. Power decides how the gains get split. That's why collective bargaining and mechanism design need each other.

Adrian, you're right that whoever meters ends up defining the right. That's why I want the meter built as an open protocol that anyone can implement and audit. Protocols are rules of the road, and they shape the market. If one company owns the meter, it becomes the next toll booth. If the meter is a protocol, many parties can witness each event.

Leslie, I take your point about legibility. It's a design requirement for any scheme like this.

For the manifesto: pay for outputs, not training. Every AI answer should disclose the sources it retrieved and cited, through open, standardized telemetry, and royalties should flow in proportion to each source's role in the answer. It works for us at O'Reilly, and the labs can afford to do it.

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Geoffrey's warning is the one I'd underline. We're building expensive, closed integrity tools that only some publishers can afford, and that shouldn't be where AI money ends up. I'm glad Amy, Leslie and Henry agree that paying per article or per token pays for volume. Selena, crediting reviewers and patrollers by name is a real start. Money is better still.

Tim and Alex, I have one concern about your meters. Right now a retracted paper counts as "used" just like a sound one. We already know retracted papers keep getting cited, and more than 90 percent of those citations don't mention the retraction. A model grounding on Reuben's faked trials would generate royalty events. So retraction status has to be part of the telemetry. Retrieving retracted work should be flagged and should never earn a payment.

Adrian, I'd add one thing to "who guards the guards." The people doing the guarding right now are unpaid sleuths, and they get harassment and lawsuits in return.

For the manifesto: any AI licensing money should include a fixed share for correcting the record. That means paying reviewers, bug-bounty payments to sleuths, and funding for open retraction data. AI systems should check that data before they answer and when they pay out. I'm not proposing this as another detection tool. The point is that finding and fixing errors becomes paid work.
